content_metadata.description: A video exploring the possibility of humans growing wings through genetic modification, discussing the scientific, ethical, and feasibility aspects.

qAndA.answer: She mentions that a human genome contains instructions for growing two arms, two legs, ten fingers, and ten toes, but not wings.
qAndA.question: What specific examples does Dr. Thornton give to illustrate the concept of a genome?

qAndA.answer: Dr. Thornton compares understanding a genome to deciphering a language that we don't fully comprehend.
qAndA.question: What is the visual analogy used to explain the complexity of understanding a genome?

qAndA.answer: She explains that modifying the genome needs to happen at a very early stage of development, making it impossible to seek consent from an unborn baby.
qAndA.question: Besides ethical considerations, what practical challenge does Dr. Thornton point out about adding wings to a human?

qAndA.answer: The ethical dilemma revolves around modifying an unborn baby's genome to give them wings, without having the ability to ask for their consent.
qAndA.question: What is the central ethical dilemma raised in the video?

qAndA.answer: The syringe animation is used to visually represent the idea of injecting genetic material (from a bat) into the human genome.
qAndA.question: What is the purpose of the syringe animation shown in the video?

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Hi, my name is Jade and I'm Lauren, we're PCS student and we're staying genetics in our class.
And we want to ask you a question.
Is it genetically possible to grow wings under back and be able to fly?
Hi, I'm Dr. Sarah Thornton and I'm a biologist here at MIT.
The question of whether we could grow wings is a really interesting one because it's very
similar to some other questions that we've answered here at Ask MIT.
If you haven't already seen the videos about how to make a unicorn or if humans could
engineer ourselves not to need any oxygen, I really recommend that you watch them after
this video.
To figure out how we would build a human with wings, we really need to start at the beginning.
How do you build a human?
How are we put together?
You may know that all living things have genomes, which are made of DNA, and are basically
the instruction manual for how to build an organism.
You just don't know 100% how to read these instruction manuals yet, like a language
that we don't totally understand.
Scientists are working on this and we understand more every single day.
We do know that you started as one cell that followed the instructions given by your genome
and divided again and again and again into trillions of cells that assembled according
to the instructions of your genome into a human.
You have two arms, two legs, ten fingers, ten toes, but no wings.
But the genome of a bat or a bird do call for wings to be added to those animals when
they develop from one bat cell to a baby bat or one bird cell to a baby bird.
We don't know enough to do this yet, but sometime in the future we'll know enough about how
to read genomes in order to identify the part of the bat genome that calls for wings and
be able to take that piece of the bat genome and put it into the human genome.
However, even if we were able to do that, the tricky part is that we can't just do it
in a child or an adult.
You're already assembled into a human being with no wings and it's too late to call for
wings when you're already fully developed.
What we would need to do is take that piece of the bat genome and put it into the genome
of a very early unborn baby.
Now this is a really tricky issue because you can't ask an unborn baby if they want
wings.
So, is it really okay to give a human wings without being able to ask their permission?
Another really big issue like this that scientists are talking a lot about right now is if
you could take that unborn baby and modify their genome so that instead of giving the wings,
you would instead cure them of a disease.
Would that be okay to do without their permission?
What do you think?
So, there's our roadmap for making a human with wings.
First, we have to understand more about how to read the genome.
Second, we have to decide whether it's okay to edit the genome of an unborn baby without
being able to ask their permission.
And then we need to take the part of the bat genome that encodes for wings and put it
into the genome of a very early unborn baby and allow that baby to grow and develop into
a human with wings.
But even if you can make a human with wings, would that human be able to fly?
Professor Prairie is going to answer the other half of your question.
